translation:
Ram Kabir is Truth; the true Guru is Truth.

The Samagam gives an outline of the life of Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj — from his manifestation (Pragatya) to his departure to his own divine abode (Swadham) — together with the teaching he received from his Guru and the teaching he gave to his own disciples, through which he established the Uda Dharma. It expounds the principles of this Uda Dharma and shows how to practise unwavering devotion (bhakti, devotion) to Vishnu free of ritualism (karmakand), and it has taught how to put this into practice in daily life.

The Samagam's chapter on the distinction between Maya and Brahm serves as an introduction to the fundamental principles of this Samagam. Now the Samagam proper begins with the chapter on the manifestation of Jivanji Maharaj; before starting it, the writing opens with a sakhi (couplet) that conveys an instruction of Jivanji Maharaj's own.

|| Sakhi ||
_Sab sakhiyan-man Radhika, sab sakhan-man Balvir |
Tahan Vyas viveki Jivana, jahan Kalindi-ki tir ||1||_
(Meaning: Just as, in Vrajbhoomi where the unbroken Ras Lila unfolds, Radhaji is the foremost among all the sakhis, and Balvir Baldevji is the foremost among the Lord's companions — so too, on the bank of the Yamuna in Vrajbhoomi, dwells Hariram Vyasdasji, the foremost devotee of Radha-Krishna, who worships Radhavallabh with unwavering devotion, with discernment and free of ritualism.)

When Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj went to Vrindavan, he stayed there four days. He met a Vaishnav there, and a goshthi (satsang, holy discourse) took place with him — this is mentioned on page 48 of the printed Samagam, though the Vaishnav's name is not given there. However, the parchari (biographical account) of Jivanji Maharaj states that this Vaishnav was Hariram Vyas, and that this sakhi is the one spoken in that parchari while praising Vyasdas. Jivanji Maharaj was so deeply moved by Vyasdas that he spoke a sakhi placing Vyasji among saints equal in stature to Kabirji.

_Dou barabar Jivana, das Kabir aru Vyas |
O samre Sitapatiko, ye Radhe kunj vilas ||2||_
(Meaning: Das Kabir and Vyas, O Jivana, are equal to one another in their unwavering devotion to Vishnu. Of the two, Kabirji is one who remembers Sitapati Ram, while Vyasji is a worshipper of Radha-Krishna who delights in the groves [kunj] of Vraj.)

Jivanji Maharaj praised Vyas highly, holding him equal in excellence to Kabir, and to Radha and Balvir, because Vyasji's views matched Jivanji Maharaj's own views very closely. Vyasji did not maintain his Brahmin identity, but was a lover devoted to Vishnu-bhakti in the tradition of the saints. He had given up the sacred thread (janoi) as well, considering it a burden; he did not believe in worship of the sun-god, nor did he accept the worship of Ganpati; nor did he observe Ekadashi or other such vows. He held to devotion to Radha-Krishna alone.

In keeping with the praise of Vyasji given within the original Samagam, the second chapter of the Bhagwat Mahatmya, at the end of the Bhagwat, describes Uddhav, the supreme devotee of Krishna, in a manner corresponding to how Vyas became a supreme devotee of Radha-Krishna on the bank of the Kalindi (Yamuna). It also describes the unbroken good fortune (saubhagya) of Kalindi-Yamuna, the Lord's chief queen. Devoted copyists who transcribed the Samagam inserted that episode into it as they wrote it, and the passage reads as follows:

The episode from the Shri Bhagwat Mahatmya is recorded here. Vajranabh, son of Aniruddha, ruled in Mathura. King Parikshit came there. Afterward, having heard the account of Krishna's life, the gopas and gopis came before Kahan [Krishna]. They were struck with wonder as to how that divine play (lila) had come to an end. Then the sage Shandilya arrived. He said to them: "Why are you so astonished? Lila is of two kinds — one is the everyday, worldly lila, and the other is the eternal, unbroken lila, in which loving devotees are united [with the Lord]. Beings of the three-gunas creation — gods, demons, and the rest — have no claim upon the eternal lila."

It is the supremely blissful, loving Vaishnav devotee who has a claim upon it. Here is an illustration of this: once, sixteen thousand one hundred (16,100) widows who had been separated from Shri Krishna came before Shri Jamunaji [the river Yamuna], who granted them darshan [sacred vision] together with the marks of good fortune (saubhagya) of a married woman. They asked her: "Our Lord Shri Krishna has departed to His own abode — why do you still bear the marks of good fortune?" Jamunaji answered: "Shri Krishna, together with Radhikaji and all the gopas and gopis, dwells forever in the eternal, unbroken lila. I am Radhika's maidservant; I am in her eternal service; I know no separation. Uddhavji has attained the gopas and gopis within that eternal lila. Uddhavji dwells, in the form of a creeper, at the foot of Govardhan hill, in the Sakhi-sthal where Kusum Sarovar is. Go there, sing kirtan (devotional hymns) of Krishna's lila, and dwell there; then Uddhavji will grant you darshan, and you too shall attain the eternal lila." Hearing these words of Jamunaji, they went to Kusum Sarovar and dwelt there, singing kirtan and bhajan. Uddhavji then appeared, radiant in his dark form; showing them his form studded with gems and jewels, he embraced them all. Then they beheld Shri Krishna — endowed with all sixteen kalas [divine attributes] — enacting the eternal lila together with Radhikaji; he delights there forever. This lila reveals itself to loving devotees.

Testimony to this is borne out in many places by the kirtans of Narsinh Mehta. This episode is narrated in many places as addressed to the sage Saunak. But it is only devotees who attain the sweetness of that lila. This passage was heard from a temple of the Gosainji of the Vallabh lineage, and it has been set down here because it was found fitting to the time and place. Thus this sakhi in praise of Vyas, presented as the heading of this Samagam, is the instruction that enjoins unwavering devotion. Who Jivanji Maharaj was is introduced within the Samagam in the chapter on Sadguru Praman [the credentials of the true Guru]; the account here begins from after his eleventh year.

In Samvat 1660, at the age of eleven, Jivanji Maharaj manifested at Gahej Goriyad for the welfare of the soul, and the dharma of Namdev and Kabir became manifest to him. A love for singing of that lila arose in him, and wherever there were Vaishnavs to discuss sakhi and shabda [scriptural teachings] with, he found delight in loving devotion (bhakti). Thus, at the age of sixteen, his first meeting took place, in the village of Keslu-ba, with Gopaldas of Chorenda of the Janak lineage, and a samagam-satsang [holy meeting] took place lasting a full day and night.

Keslu is present-day Kesru, near Paleja — so Poojya Yadunath Maharaj has written. Janakvansh and similar terms are words used, within the tradition of the Barot people, to identify their lineage. Barots for the most part follow the profession of vahivancha [genealogist and record-keeper], and they generally hail from the direction of Rajasthan. Gopaldas's guru's guru, Sukhji, is reckoned to be of the Pipavansh [Pipa's lineage]. In this way, within Barot society, different families are known by different lineage-traditions. In the Bhaktamal of Lucknow, page 667, one devotee, Lakhaji, is known as belonging to the Vanarvansh [monkey lineage]; another is known as Devvanshi. Thus the identities of Barots are known through various different lineages.

Before accepting Sadguru Gopaldas as his guru, Jivanji Maharaj discussed and deliberated the path of bhakti with him so as to be certain of it; and so, first of all, he sought to dispel the confusion between the formed (sakar) and the formless (nirakar). Two views prevail regarding God: (1) that God is sagun-sakar (possessed of attributes, and with form), and (2) that God is nirgun-nirakar (without attributes, formless). Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj asked for this to be clarified. Gopaldas then said: God's sagun-sakar form — the form composed of the five elements, the three gunas, and the senses, which is now blazing forth — is only temporary. When that form releases its own qualities — that is, when God closes and gathers back His form with attributes — then that Brahm-Parmatma-Bhagwat form ceases to be such and becomes the Atma-swaroop [form of the pure soul]; and that Atma-swaroop will, in turn, again take on the form of an individual soul (jiva). That is to say: God, having completed an avatar, dissolves into the Parmatma form, and will again in turn take up an avatar. He then spoke a sakhi concerning this.

Poojya Yadunath Maharaj says: "Dream" means the jiva [individual soul] that has lost its way through Maya; that which is awake and aware is chetan [pure consciousness], and that alone is Truth, that alone is the Beloved.

In Samvat 1660, on the eighth day (Ashtami) of the bright half of Shravan, Vaishnav Jivandasji came, for the welfare of the soul, to the village called Gahej Goriyad (Gaj), in the Kanam region of the holy heartland of Gujarat. Here the dharma of Namdev and Kabirji became manifest to him. In his eleventh year, an intense yearning to sing of that lila was awakened here in his heart.

Wherever there was a Vaishnav to discuss sakh and shabda [scriptural teaching] with, affection would grow there; and so, in his sixteenth year, a samagam took place with Gopaldasji of the Janak lineage (of Chorenda), in the village called Keslu-ba. This was their first meeting. Jivanji greeted Gopaldas with "Ram Ram." Gopaldas had come there from another village, after performing karaj [the rites performed after a death]. Jivandasji then invited him to his own mandir [home], and there they performed Hari-kirtan. On this occasion, the samagam lasted a full night and day. Afterward, Gopaldasji set out on his way back to his own home in Chorenda.
